Honestly, it’s just a checklist of clichés. You know the type: the absent piece-of-shit father who abandoned his daughter for a woman he secretly loved, or a career he tried to build, or a job he needed for money, or an adventure he wanted — anything but her. Then the whole film is him trying to make amends. His life is a wreck, so we’re supposed to see him as helpless: booze, pills, bar fights, dead-end jobs, unpaid rent, screaming matches, and self-pity. Here, the only difference is that he left her for a man (he’s gay), and instead of booze, pills, and bar fights, his rock bottom is overeating and obesity. If they’d cast a Black actor, the cliché bingo card would be full. Whatever. Even The Wrestler by the same director is the same old cliché — he basically just repeated himself.

I admit it. I don't get what Darren Aronofsky is going for anymore. Mother was a misstep with really obvious heavy handed symbolism but I thought it was a one off. I thought it was an ironic post modern joke. But the Whale has all the exact same issues. It's filled with uninteresting one dimensional characters. It's stylistically boring and derivative. And its symbolism feels like something out of a high school level creative writing seminar. And the acting is bad and I think the actors are poorly directed. It's like they've been coached to eliminate any nuances from their performances. Case in point, Samantha Morton is a great actress but she came in with a very strange accent that is weirdly off putting. And while I can kind of see how it could work, I get the sneaking suspicion that she was directed to be less subtle with it than she would be otherwise. After this and Caught Stealing I really had doubts about whether Aronofsky was ever a uniquely talented director or not. But after going through his filmography again recently I really do think this is the case of a great director who just lost his motivation to really try to make great films. He's just trying to pass as a great director.

This is especially true with Charlie’s behaviour towards Ellie. And Thomas’ character. As ugly as one’s wrongs may have been, is there enough good in one’s future actions to repay such moral debts? Apart from my praise on that aspect, I really think that the movie just fails to really be great on expanding the various points of discussion to which it outlines. Religion, healthcare, eating disorders are some of the main talking points, but if it serves to just be a backdrop to the aforementioned conscience of human beings, then it served very well. But I honestly felt like these themes are just very superficial and were only used for shock-value or to make the story more sad. The movie is disgusting, but its good and meets the mark for what its trying to go for.

critique, The Whale (2022, Darren Aronofsky) The Whale aura toujours une place particulière pour moi. C’est le premier film que j’ai vu avec la personne avec qui je suis encore aujourd’hui. À l’époque, je ne savais absolument pas ce que j’allais regarder. Je ne connaissais quasiment rien du film, je ne savais pas à quoi m’attendre, et pourtant j’avais adoré. Forcément, le revoir aujourd’hui est assez particulier. Parce que même si j’ai toujours beaucoup d’affection pour ce film, je l’ai trouvé beaucoup moins intéressant et surtout beaucoup moins touchant que lors de mon premier visionnage. Pourtant, son sujet continue énormément de me toucher. Je n’ai jamais vécu une situation aussi extrême que celle de Charlie, mais je comprends certaines choses dans ce qu’il traverse, notamment cette solitude, cette culpabilité et cette impression d’être complètement enfermé dans sa propre vie. Mais avec le recul, j’ai aussi beaucoup plus vu les défauts du film. J’ai notamment trouvé l’écriture beaucoup trop appuyée par moments. Certains dialogues donnent parfois l’impression que les personnages doivent absolument expliquer ce qu’ils ressentent, alors que les situations auraient parfois été beaucoup plus fortes si le film avait simplement laissé les émotions parler d’elles-mêmes. J’ai aussi eu du mal avec certains personnages. Je les trouve intéressants sur le papier, mais parfois trop écrits comme des moyens de faire avancer le drame. Certaines réactions m’ont paru excessives, et ça m’a empêché de croire complètement à certaines scènes. Et puis il y a le côté très mélodramatique du film. Lors de mon premier visionnage, ça m’avait énormément touché. Aujourd’hui, j’ai davantage ressenti la volonté du film de me faire pleurer. Et forcément, ça fonctionne beaucoup moins sur moi. En revanche, Brendan Fraser reste vraiment excellent. Sa performance est impressionnante, et il arrive à rendre Charlie profondément humain malgré tous ses défauts et toutes ses contradictions. J’aime aussi beaucoup le huis clos. Le fait de rester quasiment tout le temps dans cet appartement renforce cette impression d’enfermement. Charlie est prisonnier de son corps, mais aussi de ses choix, de son passé et de la vie qu’il a construite autour de lui. C’est probablement ce qui me touche encore le plus dans le film. Mais aujourd’hui, je ne peux plus dire que j’ai adoré The Whale. Je garde énormément d’affection pour lui, forcément, parce qu’il est lié à un souvenir qui compte énormément pour moi. Mais si je mets complètement ce souvenir de côté, je trouve simplement que c’est un film bien moins subtil et moins bouleversant que dans mes souvenirs. Je suis content de l’avoir revu. Même si, finalement, je crois que je préfère le souvenir que j’en avais.

A Baleia foi um filme que me deixou desconfortável de uma maneira que eu acho que era exatamente a intenção. O Charlie é um homem que está vivendo os últimos momentos da própria vida e sabe disso. Ele está extremamente doente, isolado e preso dentro de uma rotina que parece ter diminuído até quase desaparecer. Mas o filme não começa tratando Charlie como uma pessoa monstruosa ou como alguém que merece aquilo. Ele mostra um homem cheio de arrependimentos. A relação dele com a filha Ellie é provavelmente a parte mais dolorosa. Ela é cruel com ele. Mas a crueldade dela não aparece simplesmente porque ela é uma adolescente "má". Existe uma história inteira de abandono, raiva e ressentimento por trás. Charlie sabe que falhou. E ele não tenta convencer Ellie de que não falhou. Ele simplesmente quer uma última oportunidade de fazer alguma coisa certa. A atuação do Brendan Fraser é realmente impressionante porque grande parte da interpretação está no rosto e na voz. Existe uma tristeza muito profunda nele. E a câmera também ajuda muito. O formato quase fechado faz o espectador sentir aquela sensação de confinamento. Tudo parece apertado. O apartamento. O corpo. A vida. As possibilidades. E talvez seja justamente isso que torne o filme tão difícil. Charlie não está tentando salvar a própria vida. Ele está tentando encontrar algum significado antes que ela termine. E quando o filme chega ao final, eu não sinto exatamente alívio. Sinto tristeza. Mas também sinto uma espécie de compaixão por alguém que passou tanto tempo acreditando que não merecia ser perdoado. É um filme sobre culpa, mas também sobre a necessidade humana de acreditar que ainda podemos ser vistos como pessoas depois de cometer erros. E acho que essa é a parte que mais fica comigo depois que os créditos sobem.

Who's afraid of a protagonist who is abjectly fat and also morally deplorable? Seemingly many. The discourse is long-winding and diverse yet I think the utter disgust of The Whale, an adapted play of ugly emotional outpouring, the revival of a viscous past, and certainly nothing beautiful to look at visually, irks many in their yearning for a harmony in a story that rewards beauty and deplores the ugly. Charlie is a psychologically beguiling character who embodies a descend into gluttony and sloth, an active manifestation of a desire to withdraw following loss, which renders him a simultaneous victim and perpetrator of avoidance to those around him. His struggle with obesity is almost framed as a carnal punishment for his immediate act of gluttony, pursuing his forbidden sexuality and escaping with his lover; he is burdened with the consequences of his withdrawal, his wife brandishes him a deadbeat and his daughter wants nothing but his eternal damnation in grease-laced hellfire. The Whale is a manifestation of the deadly sins of the human condition to some degree, with Charlie representing a combination of sloth and gluttony (although I think to simply demarcate Charlie along his patterns of eating would be reductive, as I'll explain), while his daughter is wrathful, her deep-seated anger and intention for immediate action contrasting with Charlie's inertia. Charlie's obesity could've been replaced with another gluttonous issue, alcoholism, drugs and the same point could've been made, not to say that I disagree with the film's execution, in fact I laud them for tackling subject matter usually addressed humorously (haha, look upon the perils of this fat fuck and laugh!), for there's countless films about alcoholics. Charlie suffers from a binge eating disorder as a result of trauma, and as a result of his disposition, conflict-avoidant and seeking constant pleasure (the film is framed by Charlie masturbating, and there are constant scenes of his consumption of sugar, an infatuation with sweetness and ecstasy), he is unable to graduate from these harmful patterns, ultimately swallowing himself, and those around him up. Charlie is not only victimising on himself, wrapped in the twine of masochism, he performs these rites disgustingly just by existing, which I think explains the critical upset people have at this to some degree. His visual pain is horrible to witness, he is unable to be romanticised, for to be fat is to be abject, to be alienated from society's metanarrative over aesthetical beauty. The hegemonic power of beauty deserts our protagonist, leaving him unable to be sympathised with or related to, no pretty edits will be made of his suffering, only edits that lampoon his story as something hilarious and ironic. Such is the state of the modern consumer of the arts. Death can function as a wonderful writing device for the extraction, the confession of truth, in fact the confines of the setting slowly pluck the truth out of the characters. The news of Charlie's imminent death spread from Liz to Charlie, to Ellie and Thomas, and then eventually his ex-wife Mary; the epistemic revelation suddenly compels people to discover the truth before the horrid inevitable occurs, the story an eventual confession chamber for deep-seated reservations and emotions. Perhaps, the film is quite blatant in its expressions, lacking subtlety (there's an almost laughable lack of such in Ellie's dialogue, demarcating her intentions almost constantly, that she wants this or wants that). The film does not narrate with its environment or through non-verbal expressions so much as it does with loud, confessional-style dialogue and discussions of context surrounding the emotions we see splattered on the wooden floor. It has its benefits, yet at times I did feel that how the characters felt could've been handled more delicately, allowed to fester for much longer. The Whale prides itself on having nothing left unsaid, especially reflected in Charlie's motivations. Death performs a latent function as something that unites people, as Charlie notes almost humorously; all of his cherished ones unite, only at the advent of his demise, after years of stifled truths and assumptions. The ritual of death allows the ones that are left to unite for a cause, that of the lamentation and memorialisation of the deceased. The morbidity is the most beautiful aspect, and for that I cannot help but view The Whale with beauty in its morbidity and reflection of the grimy reality. The stone is overturned to reveal bile that has festered for what appears to be forever.

All the characters are coping with depression here in one way or another. Liz is enabling Charlie. Charlie with his emotional eating. Ellie in acting out, being cruel to feel cold and emotionless, Thomas struggling with God and essentially his own self, his morals. The Whale is desperation of individuals trapped inside their own emotional prisons. Every single person in that apartment is deeply flawed and at times actively difficult to like, yet the story makes their defense mechanisms feel entirely earned. Watching Charlie's gentle optimism clash against his slow self-destruction, or seeing Ellie's cruelty contextually understood as a shield for her abandonment. Hong Chau’s character represents the tragedy of codependency. Terrified of losing another person after her brother Alan's suicide, her caretaking morphs into enabling. She brings Charlie high-calorie food while simultaneously taking his blood pressure. Her love is undeniable, but her trauma makes her an accomplice to his destruction. Thomas attempts to frame Charlie's condition as a spiritual crisis rather than a human one. Running from his own personal failures, he uses evangelism as a distraction, attempting to "save" Charlie in order to validate his own shaky moral compass. Sadie Sink’s character handles depression through rage. Feeling abandoned by her father, she projects a cold, malicious exterior to ensure no one can hurt her again. Throughout the film, Charlie repeatedly listens to an essay analyzing Herman Melville’s Moby-Dick. The essay points out that Melville wrote about whales extensively just to distract the reader from his own sad story. Moby Dick is the motif to talk all about how we all distract ourselves from ourselves to not feel the pain. Charlie’s entire career as an online English teacher revolves around begging his students to "write something honest". He sees society constantly putting up "pasteboard masks” to hide ugly, uncomfortable feelings. The Moby-Dick essay represents the one piece of pure, unvarnished honesty Charlie holds onto. When he forces Ellie to read it to him in the climax, it becomes a moment of mutual liberation. By acknowledging the sadness and loneliness in the book, Ellie acknowledges her own, allowing Charlie to finally let go and float upward, stripped of the literal and metaphorical weight that anchored him. The final moment directly ties back to Ellie’s essay. She wrote that Melville’s book was about confronting sadness directly rather than hiding behind distractions. By confronting the truth of their relationship and reading the essay together, both Charlie and Ellie stop hiding. Charlie got what he wanted, doing one good thing about his life. He doesn’t die in despair but rather dies liberated and so he vanishes into the white.

"Lucien, why did it happen? Why did he let it happen?" "Let it, Matthew? I think he did a little more than let it happen. Charitably, I think, sometimes, perhaps, one must change or die. And, in the end, there were, perhaps, limits to how much he would let himself change." - Neil Gaiman, "The Sandman: The Wake" The Whale is about people's inability to be honest with themselves and the terrible, often fatal, consequences of that failure. Charlie (Brendan Fraser) is eating himself to death out of guilt. He abandoned his wife and daughter to shack up with a gay lover 8 years ago. After a few happy years together, his lover, who was brought up in an evangelical Christian household, could no longer bear the shame of his homosexuality and committed suicide. Charlie started binge-eating shortly after. Today (early 2016 in the film's setting, during the tumultuous Republican primaries that Donald Trump ultimately won), he suffers from congestive heart failure and has weeks, possibly days, left to live. His nurse Liz (the adopted sister of his lover) begs him to check into the hospital and save himself, but Charlie refuses, spuriously citing his lack of insurance. But he, Liz, and we the viewer all know that he wants to die. His imminent end decided, he sets out to make amends with his wife and daughter so he can die in peace. This central theme of "change or die" is most vividly expressed by Charlie, but it's also visible in every other character, who act as foils for him - * Alan, Charlie's aforementioned lover, was unable to exorcise the ghost of Christian dogma and pays for it with both his life and indirectly Charlie's. * Thomas, an evangelical missionary on a personal crusade to convert Charlie on his deathbed, is on the run from his church after embezzling from them and faces imminent homelessness because he's too ashamed to reach out to his father. * Ellie, Charlie's daughter, is about to flunk out of school because she won't stop acting out (a common situation for children who grow up in fatherless homes). * Mary, Charlie's ex-wife (played by Samantha Morton, an actress who's haunted my dreams since her turn in Synecdoche New York), is unable to move on from Charlie and create a good family life for Ellie, chaining both of them to the past. * Liz, Charlie's nurse, enables Charlie's behavior because Alan (her brother) starved himself before his suicide and she can't bear to stop Charlie eating. There's also a racial undercurrent which I enjoyed. Liz (Charlie's Asian nurse) and Dan (Charlie's Indian pizza delivery man) perform hard labor that lets Charlie work a cushy laptop job (teaching English classes online with the camera off) while he kills himself slowly by stuffing his repulsive fat face. This works as a metaphor for both the global economy (93% of the world toil so the 7% that's white can role-play that they're in a movie) and for COVID (which was ongoing during filming). Framing the film's narrative is an essay written by Charlie's daughter Ellie about "Moby Dick, or, The Whale" when she was in the eighth grade. (It's a brilliant metaphor, but reading the unabridged Moby Dick is too much for 95% of adults. There's zero chance a 13-year-old capable of this would ever flunk out of school.) Charlie serves as Ishmael, Ahab, and Moby Dick in this allegory. Ishmael was him prior to Alan's death, Ahab is his soul trapped and seeking absolution through death, and Moby Dick is his diseased, bloated, white body which he longs to slay. But the most haunting part of The Whale by far is the ending 10 minutes, which I've rewatched a number of times now. Charlie lies dying on the couch, and Ellie arrives to confront him one last time. He begs her to read him her essay, to which she responds by insulting him, flinging open the door, and preparing to storm off. But she changes her mind, turns around, looks Charlie dead in the eye, and starts reading. Charlie, in a final dying burst of strength, lifts himself to his feet unassisted (which he was incapable of the whole film prior) and stumbles toward her on lymphedema-ridden legs. She finishes, smiles at him, he smiles back, and then he levitates off the ground as white light engulfs him and he dies content. I desperately want the past paragraph to be true, but I believe that it was all happening inside Charlie's head. After your heart stops because of a fatal heart attack, your brain still functions for a few minutes as it loses oxygen. Many people who have been brought back to life after such near-death experiences report a feeling of euphoria and peace and light. Charlie suffered a massive heart attack as his daughter cussed him out and then left him to die alone. His final redemptive meeting with her was entirely in his head, a dying man's hallucinations as his brain shuts down. In light of this information, The Whale serves as an emphatic warning. Don't let your relationships with your loved ones wither away. Our time is limited and our bodies are pathetically fragile. It's later than you think.

Never have i ever had to hold back tears in science class. But far out if this one was making it pretty hard. I wouldn't normally say that i get emotional watching movies but this one wow. What started as a bumpy ride from the start with seeing the grotesque figure of Charlie scoffing down food, struggling to walk and then the opening scene literally watching him have a wank, I had no idea what i was getting myself into. But i pushed past all the sad eating montages and the sobs of charlie and then what i was rewarded with by the end was one of the most beautiful endings to a film I think ive ever watched. The one room setting of charlie's apartment along with the 3:4 aspect ratio created this really claustrophobic effect and setting which complimented the themes of the film. Since the film was majority set in Charlie's apartment when the setting changed symbolically you knew something significant symbolically was going to happen. to continue ranting on about sets and lighting, I loved the orange and teal lighting from fluorescent lights around the house i dont think it created anything like symbolic but I just enjoyed the atmosphere it created. And oh my god the framing of some of the scenes especially the one with the church boy thomas and the friend/ caretaker Liz outside of the apartment. Symmetry and the set design blocking and just like everything was perfect. I also loved how few characters there were but how each of them kind of brought a different significance to the story and helped the viewers understand the story of Charlies life. Brendan Fraser oscar was definitely deserved but HOW GOOD WAS THE SCORE FOR THIS FILM!!!! i'm checking it now and it didn't even get nominated for that as an award but props to the musicians who cooked up heart string pulling music that I think drove the whole film and made Brendan Fraser's performance so breathtaking. 10/10 definitely a movie must watched
